blocks.5e012d6e: As we said above, the naive Bayes model is a type of Bayesian network. Its graph structure has the class variable as the root, and the class variable is the only "parent" of all the feature variables.
blocks.cc87cb4f: Bayesian networks are a family of models. They are part of a more general category: (probabilistic) graphical models. Graphical models are a modelling "language" for probabilistic models. They are powerful mainly for two reasons: i) they can show domains with many variables and complex dependencies in a compact form, and ii) there are efficient inference procedures that use the structure of the models.
blocks.cfdd3fd0: A Bayesian network shows a joint distribution over some random variables. The Bayesian network can need much fewer numerical parameters than the number of elementary events in the domain. This depends on the complexity of the network, that is, on the number and the positions of the edges in the graph.
blocks.0c281e26: The structure of the network is a graph. Each random variable is a node. A set of directed edges between the nodes shows the structure of the dependencies. The graph must be a directed acyclic graph (DAG). This means that you cannot start from a node, follow a path in the direction of the edges, and get back to the same node.

blocks.10a4981e: The random variables in the model are X, Y, Z and Å. (If you are not from Scandinavia: in Finland, we call the last letter the "Swedish O"; see Wikipedia:Å. In our alphabet, it comes after X, Y and Z, which is convenient.) The edges show direct dependency. Thus, when there is no edge between two variables, the variables are conditionally independent, given some (possibly empty) set of other variables. The details of this are a little too complex to discuss here, so we do not look at them. For now, remember only that the edges show the structure of the dependencies in the domain.
blocks.9d96824e: A Bayesian network has the structure (the DAG), and it also has a set of parameters for the conditional distributions of the variables. These parameters have the form P(V = v \mid \mathrm{Pa}_V = \mathrm{pa}_V). Here, V is a random variable, v is a value, and \mathrm{Pa}_V is the set of parents of the node V in the graph: that is, the nodes that have an edge to V. For example, in the DAG above, \mathrm{Pa}_Z = \{X, Y\}, and \mathrm{Pa}_Y = \emptyset, because the node Y has no parents.
blocks.0ce260bd: When the variables are categorical (that is, their values are in a finite set), we can give the conditional distributions as conditional probability tables (CPTs). A CPT for the variable V contains the distribution of V for each possible combination of the values of the parents of V. We call these combinations parent configurations. For example, if all variables in the example network above are binary, the parent configurations of Z are (X=0, Y=0), (X=0, Y=1), (X=1, Y=0), (X=1, Y=1). Thus, the CPT of Z has four rows, and each row contains a conditional distribution for Z. This is a real example:
blocks.46cd7f55: For example, if X = 1 and Y = 0, the conditional probability of Z = 1 is P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1, Y = 0) = 0.5, and so on.
blocks.e077759e: For a variable that has no parents in the network, the CPT is only one distribution, and it has only one row. For variables that have many parents, the CPT can easily become very, very large.

blocks.f1b71d13: Machine learning is the scientific study of algorithms that improve automatically from experience.
blocks.cbdd44de: During the Second World War, Alan Turing worked to decrypt messages that the German military encoded with the Enigma machine. To decipher these messages, it was necessary to test a very large number of possibilities. This task was difficult for humans, but machines could do it quite quickly. (The machines against Enigma, the Bombes, were electromechanical devices, not computers. The first programmable electronic computer, Colossus, was used from 1944 against a different German cipher, Lorenz.) But we cannot solve all problems that are difficult for humans efficiently with a programmed algorithm. For NP-hard problems, nobody knows an algorithm that solves each instance in polynomial time. Such an algorithm does not exist unless P = NP, which is a famous open question. On their most difficult instances, all known exact methods need exponential time. No computer can do miracles to get past this limit. But clever algorithms and heuristics can still solve many practical instances, exactly or approximately.
blocks.c4a4d3ef: There is also an interesting class of problems that humans solve easily, but that are very difficult to write as a computer program. Examples are:
blocks.f058efc8: Translate text from one language to a different language;
blocks.71d3fd44: Compare two documents on the internet to find which one is more relevant to a search query;
blocks.f135fa1e: Estimate the sale price of a property.
blocks.1142509b: These problems have some common properties:
blocks.05a7efca: Function Representation: often, we can write the solutions as a function that maps inputs (also called samples) to outputs (also called targets). For example, we can map patients to diagnoses, and documents to relevance scores.
blocks.c8a8abcb: No Perfect Solution: these problems usually do not have one ideal solution. For example, professional translators can make different translations of the same text, and both can be correct. Also, doctors sometimes make an incorrect diagnosis, and people can interpret an image differently.
blocks.141d7c34: Labeled Examples: often, we have many examples of correct solutions (for example, translations of sentences into a different language, or images with labels). If we need examples of incorrect solutions, it is usually easy to make them.
blocks.99a24597: In machine learning, the function that maps objects to predictions is a model. The set of labelled examples is the training dataset (or training set). A training dataset contains:
blocks.5d93d6e2: Objects: for example, images from the internet, medical histories of patients, or data about what users do in a service;
blocks.ea27e205: Labels (or targets): for example, captions for images, diagnoses, or information about the behaviour of users. These are the outputs that the model learns to predict.
blocks.6dbcf788: The tasks above are examples of supervised learning problems, because we know the correct answers (targets) for each object in the training dataset before the training. We put supervised learning tasks into groups by the type of the set Y, which contains all possible answers (targets):
blocks.af21f92e: Regression (Y = \mathbb{R} or Y = \mathbb{R}^M): in regression tasks, the target values are continuous. Examples are to predict the duration of a car-sharing trip, to estimate the demand for a specific product on a given day, or to forecast the weather in a city (for example temperature, humidity and pressure as a vector of continuous values).
blocks.98925ea7: Binary Classification (Y = \{0, 1\}): in binary classification, we predict one of two possible results. Examples: will a user click on an advertisement? Will a client pay back a loan on time? Will a student pass the exams? Will a patient get a specific condition? Is there a banana in an image?
blocks.a667ec77: Multiclass Classification (Y = \{1, \dots, K\}): multiclass classification puts each object into one of K possible classes. For example, it puts scientific articles into subject domains such as mathematics, biology or psychology.
blocks.92ef8f62: Multilabel Classification (Y = \{0, 1\}^K): in multilabel classification, an object can be in more than one class at the same time. For example, we give tags to a restaurant, and more than one tag (for example "Italian" and "Vegetarian") can be correct at the same time.
blocks.5779b8aa: Ranking: in ranking tasks, we put objects in order by relevance or by a different metric for comparison. The training labels are often relevance grades from a finite, ordered set (for example Y = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}). But the output is an order of the objects. A usual example is the ranking of the results of a search engine, where the documents are in the order of their relevance to a query. Important: the relevance score has a meaning only when we compare two documents. It has no meaning as an absolute value.
blocks.03f6bda6: More complex types of output are also possible. For example:
blocks.50e53d74: Image Segmentation: predict to which object, or type of object, each pixel in an image belongs.
blocks.19caa071: Machine Translation: make sentences (or full texts) in one language as translations of an input text in a different language.
blocks.eda3b878: Generative Modeling: make new realistic objects, from nothing or from existing data. Examples are to make the resolution of images better, or to put Snapchat or Instagram filters on faces.
blocks.9b629356: In self-supervised learning, the targets come from the data itself. For example, we hide a word in a sentence and train the model to predict it. This is how the large language models and other foundation models of Week 5 are pretrained on very large amounts of text without labels. Last, in reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error from rewards, not from correct answers. We look at it again in Week 6.

blocks.74fdc5c0: A model is a framework or a representation that describes the world. For example, the idea "the Earth is flat" is a model, and it is not as bad as it looks. This model is often useful for things at the scale of one city, where we can ignore the curvature of the Earth. But if we try to calculate the shortest route from Paris to Los Angeles, the flat-Earth model gives incorrect results, which do not agree with the data that we have. In such cases, we must replace it with a more accurate model, for example "the Earth is round" or "the Earth is an ellipsoid". This depends on the precision that we need and on the limits of our measurement tools.
blocks.775ee91e: For example, a very precise model, such as "the Earth is similar to a geoid with surface irregularities for the mountain ranges", is very good for some applications. But for most practical tasks, this level of detail can be too complex, and it can need too much computation.

blocks.f661464d: Possibly, it looks like we said that machine learning is more difficult than it is. For each machine learning task, we can make a "perfect" model: it only memorizes all of the training dataset with its labels. blocks.33c49099: Shallow trees have few parameters. Thus, they can find only high-level statistics of the training subset. These statistics are similar in all subsets, but they do not describe the target dependency in detail. Thus, the predictions on test objects are stable but not accurate (low variance, high bias).
blocks.631e9153: Deep trees are different: they can memorize the training subset in detail. Thus, the predictions on test objects change much with the training subset, but on average they are near to the true value (high variance, low bias).
blocks.b445f361: When we limit the number of features for the training of each tree, we also control the quality of the random forest. When we use more features, the correlation between the trees is higher, and the ensemble gives less benefit. When we use fewer features, each tree becomes weaker.
blocks.2972fc2a: Practical Recommendation: for classification, use the square root of the total number of features. For regression, use one-third of the features.
blocks.f2854fa3: We showed before that more base algorithms in the ensemble decrease the variance, but do not change the bias. But the trees are trained on overlapping data, so they are correlated. Thus, the variance cannot decrease without limit. If each tree has the variance \sigma^2, and the correlation between two trees is \rho, the variance of the average of B trees is \rho\sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\,\sigma^2 / B. When B increases, this goes to \rho\sigma^2, not to zero. More trees do not cause overfitting. They only need more computation. We recommend that you make a plot of the error as a function of the number of trees, and that you limit the size of the forest when the error stops decreasing much.
blocks.6fe98aae: Another practical limit is the run time of the ensemble. But we can make and use random forests in parallel. This decreases the computation time when there are many processors. But the number of processors is probably much smaller than the number of trees, and the trees are usually deep. Thus, a large random forest can need more time than we want. Then it can be a good option to use fewer trees, and to lose a little accuracy.
blocks.2a78586b: Boosting is an ensemble method. Like the methods above, it makes many base algorithms from the same family and combines them into a stronger model. The important difference is the training process:
blocks.e5b11dbb: In bagging and random forests, the base algorithms are trained independently and in parallel.
blocks.b1c64677: In boosting, the base algorithms are trained one after the other.
blocks.3ec0b3c6: In boosting, each new base algorithm is trained to decrease the total error of all the algorithms before it. Thus, the final ensemble usually has lower bias than each base algorithm alone (the variance can also decrease).
blocks.ae8e806c: The main goal of boosting is to decrease the bias. Thus, people often select base algorithms with high bias and low variance. For example, if the base classifiers are decision trees, they must usually be shallow. AdaBoost often uses stumps with one split. Gradient boosting libraries use a few levels by default, for example 3 in scikit-learn and 6 in XGBoost and CatBoost.
blocks.099edb5e: Another important reason to select models with high bias as base algorithms is that they train faster. This is very important for training one after the other, because it can need much computation if each iteration trains a complex model.
blocks.2dd68663: Now, the form of boosting that people use most in practice is gradient boosting. A separate section discusses it in detail.
blocks.0aae3bcd: Random forests are powerful, and it is quite easy to understand and implement them. But in practical applications, they are often worse than gradient boosting. Thus, gradient boosting has become the usual solution for tabular data. In domains with homogeneous data types, for example images or text, neural networks are the best.
